items.title: Event Risk Has a Price Now: Prediction Markets Join the Capital Markets
items.body:
Event Risk Has a Price Now: Prediction Markets Join the Capital Markets

Every portfolio carries risks that no stock, bond or futures contract prices directly: an election that rewrites tax law, a central bank decision that reprices everything, a hurricane that closes a coastline. For decades, investors hedged those exposures with proxies, assets that might move the right way when the event landed. Prediction markets have started selling the thing itself: a contract that pays precisely when the event happens, and nothing when it does not.

The capital has noticed. Combined monthly volume on Kalshi and Polymarket grew from under $5 billion in September 2025 to about $24 billion by April 2026, according to Jefferies figures. In February 2026, Intercontinental Exchange launched Polymarket Signals and Sentiment, packaging prediction-market odds, with historical data for backtesting, as a data product for professional investors. Tradeweb distributes Kalshi event-contract data, FIS is building clearing infrastructure, and Clear Street and Interactive Brokers have integrated Kalshi contracts for their clients.

The credibility test came from the Federal Reserve itself. A February 2026 Federal Reserve Board working paper found Kalshi's macroeconomic markets deliver well-calibrated, rapidly updating forecasts, and that on the day before each Fed meeting, the market's median and most likely outcome had a perfect record, a statistically significant improvement over fed funds futures, the instrument professionals have used for decades. When the market that prices an event beats the market that merely correlates with it, the event contract stops being a curiosity and becomes a benchmark.

Institutions are now building the pipes to use it at size. In August 2026, Cantor Fitzgerald began offering institutional block trading on Kalshi to roughly 3,000 institutional clients, with Susquehanna providing pricing and liquidity, including custom contracts for bespoke risks that traditional insurance does not cover. Kalshi's clearinghouse has also asked the CFTC to permit margin for qualified self-clearing members; event contracts are currently fully collateralized, which ties up capital for months on long-dated hedges. Kalshi has said its institutional trading volume rose more than 800% in six months.

Plenty of hedge funds are still watching rather than trading: liquidity in long-dated contracts remains thin, and standardization is young. But the direction is set. A market that began as a forecasting toy now clears institutional block trades, feeds the world's largest exchange operator's data business, and out-forecasts the futures pit on the Fed. Event risk has a price now, quoted in cents, and capital markets are learning to read it.

Sources: Sikt Intelligence; PYMNTS; Jefferies; Federal Reserve Board; Cantor Fitzgerald

items.title: Biased Traders, Honest Prices: The Psychology Inside Prediction Markets
items.body:
Biased Traders, Honest Prices: The Psychology Inside Prediction Markets

Every trader who opens a prediction market brings the same equipment: a human brain, with its factory-installed biases. We fall for the favorite-longshot bias, paying too much for improbable outcomes because the payoff feels exciting. We are overconfident in our own read of the news, we overweight whatever happened this morning, and we herd into whatever price is already moving. If markets were made of our individual judgments, the prices would be a mess. Mostly, they are not.

The biases are not theory; they are measurable in the tape. In a 2026 study of 72.1 million Kalshi trades, contracts bought at one cent won just 0.43% of the time against a 1% implied probability, meaning longshot buyers overpaid by more than half. At five cents, the win rate was 4.18% against 5% implied. There is also a YES optimism tax: traders disproportionately buy the affirmative side, and YES contracts underperformed NO at 69 of 99 price levels. Dollar-weighted, YES buyers earned excess returns of -1.02% while NO buyers earned +0.83%, a gap of nearly two points paid for the privilege of agreeing.

The losses are not evenly shared; they flow in a predictable direction. Karl Whelan's study of more than 300,000 Kalshi contracts found an average pre-fee return of roughly -20%, concentrated among takers, the traders who cross the spread with market orders, and among longshot buyers. Makers, the traders who rest limit orders and wait, earned positive returns. On Polymarket, across 588 million trades, the top 1% of accounts captured about 76.5% of the profit, predominantly by providing liquidity. The crowd's biases are, in effect, a standing transfer from the impatient to the patient.

So why does the final price stay honest? Because the mechanism taxes exaggeration. A poll costs nothing to answer; a position costs money to be wrong, and that single fact disciplines overconfidence, anchoring and herding better than any survey design. Biased flows also cancel: for every recency-driven buyer chasing the headline there is a maker happy to sell into the spike. Kalshi Research, grading 686,272 trades, found the market's closing prices scored a Brier score of 0.063, accuracy that rivals professional forecasting operations. The bias lives at the tails and in the taking. The price in the middle belongs to whoever was willing to be bored and right.

The lesson is not that prediction markets have cured human psychology. It is that they have built a machine that runs on it. The probability on the screen is the crowd's mind after its worst impulses have been charged a fee, and the toll is paid, trade after trade, by whoever insists on being the hero of the story instead of its bookmaker.

Sources: Becker Kalshi trade study (2026); Whelan, Makers and Takers, CEPR; Kalshi Research; Polymarket maker-taker study, SSRN

items.title: Polymarket Moves In: Phemex Puts Prediction Markets Inside the Exchange
items.body:
Polymarket Moves In: Phemex Puts Prediction Markets Inside the Exchange

Prediction markets no longer ask traders to come to them. Phemex, a cryptocurrency exchange, launched a Prediction Market feature today, November 2, built on Polymarket infrastructure — binary event contracts inside the same account its users already trade from, with no separate wallet and no gas fees, settled in USDT.

The first board is short-horizon crypto: YES or NO positions on the price moves of Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana and HYPE, across windows from five minutes to four hours. Shares settle at $1 or $0 against published criteria, positions can be traded before resolution, and markets resolve automatically — the full prediction-market machine, compressed into a trading app's side tab.

The design choice matters more than the asset list. Every embedded launch removes the two steps that kept event contracts niche: funding a new venue and learning a new interface. The balance, the login and the habits are already there; the contract is just one more instrument on the screen.

Phemex is the second distribution deal in four days. On October 30, mobile brokerage Aries put ForecastEx contracts on the 2026 midterms, economic data and financial markets inside its app — a different pipe, a CFTC-regulated exchange instead of Polymarket's rails, but the same strategy: meet traders where their money already sits.

The fight for 2027 is over the front door. The big exchanges keep the deepest books, but the embedded venues are competing on access and speed — and a five-minute Bitcoin contract inside an app a trader already opens every day is a hard product to out-advertise.

Sources: Traders Union, Prediction News

items.title: 358,236 Markets, One Verdict: The Price Is Usually Right
items.body:
358,236 Markets, One Verdict: The Price Is Usually Right

Prediction markets finally have a report card big enough to trust. PredictDesks graded 358,236 resolved markets, 333,464 on Polymarket and 24,772 on Kalshi, against what actually happened. A day before resolution, the favourite won 76.9% of the time, and in standard markets the average gap between price and reality was just 0.9 points on Polymarket and 1.7 on Kalshi.

Strip out the easy questions and the picture sharpens. Two-thirds of Polymarket's sampled markets resolved No, most of them long shots parked at a cent or two. Limit the test to markets priced between 10% and 90% a day out, the genuinely uncertain ones, and the favourite's win rate falls to 65.9%. The headline accuracy is real, but it is flattered by questions nobody was ever unsure about.

What is being forecast matters more than where. Tech and science markets scored a Brier 0.040 a day out on Polymarket; sports, the biggest category on both platforms, scored 0.196, the hardest call on the board. Weighted to the same mix of topics, the two exchanges finished in a dead heat: 0.150 for Polymarket, 0.147 for Kalshi. Across 24 Federal Reserve meetings priced on both, their odds differed by just 0.8 points a day before the decision.

The warning is aimed at the industry's fastest-growing product: templated ladder markets, temperature brackets, spreads, totals and exact scores, now 38% of the sample and 47% of Polymarket's 2026 markets. There, outcomes priced under 10 cents won 1.6 times as often as their prices implied, and favourites priced at 80 to 90 cents won only 76% of the time. In standard markets, long shots were the leak: every $100 spent on contracts below 5 cents returned about $81, before fees.

The rarest line in the data may be the most honest: in just 1.1% of markets, the winner had been priced at 10% or less a day earlier, a list that includes the election of Pope Leo XIV. The crowd is usually right. The study's gift is showing exactly where it is not.

Sources: PredictDesks

items.title: October Was a $128 Billion Month
items.body:
October Was a $128 Billion Month

October was not a breakout month for prediction markets. It was a step change. Traders moved $128.0 billion in contracts across the tracked exchanges in October, up 63 percent from September on a like-for-like basis, according to DeFi Rate.

Kalshi did most of it. The exchange handled $95.5 billion over the Oct. 2 to Oct. 31 window, about 76 percent of all volume, and grew 55 percent against the prior 30 days. Polymarket US was second at $14.6 billion, up 62 percent, while Polymarket's international exchange added $5.1 billion.

The growth underneath matters more than the total. Underdog Exchange was the fastest-growing venue, up 161 percent, followed by DraftKings Predictions at 126 percent and Novig at 118 percent. Nine venues now share the board, and the challengers are growing faster than the leader.

The calendar shows why. An average Sunday traded $5.2 billion, more than double an average Monday at $2.4 billion, and the busiest day in the last 60 was Sunday, Oct. 25, at $7.14 billion. Sports took 68 percent of the dollars paid on single markets, with crypto next at 25 percent.

Sources: DeFi Rate

items.title: 70 Percent, a Record: Two Days Out, the Market Prices a Sweep
items.body:
70 Percent, a Record: Two Days Out, the Market Prices a Sweep

Kalshi's balance-of-power contract put the chance of Democrats winning both the House and the Senate at 70 percent on Sunday, an all-time high and up more than nine points in a month. Polymarket priced the same sweep at 72 percent. In early September the Kalshi contract sat below 50 percent.

The alternatives are fading. A split Congress, with Democrats taking the House and Republicans retaining the Senate, priced at 27 percent on Kalshi and 23 percent on Polymarket. A Republican sweep priced at 6 percent on Kalshi and 5 percent on Polymarket.

The chamber math explains the gap. Kalshi put Democratic control of the House at 93.2 percent and the Senate at 71 percent, with Polymarket at 72 percent on the Senate. DeFi Rate put the combined Senate price up six points this week. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and the 51st seat runs through Maine, where Troy Jackson priced at 69 percent, up eight points in seven days.

The money and the ballots are moving together. Traders put $17 million into election markets in the past 24 hours, according to DeFi Rate. Of 53.9 million early ballots cast, 46 percent came from Democrats and 35 percent from Republicans. Nate Silver's generic ballot showed Democrats ahead by 9.1 points, 52.4 percent to 43.3 percent.

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. Two days out, the market is not pricing a close finish for control of Congress. It is pricing a sweep, at a record price, and leaving the split outcome as the only real alternative.

Sources: Kalshi News, DeFi Rate, Seeking Alpha

items.title: Maryland Said No. Traders Traded Its Elections Anyway
items.body:
Maryland Said No. Traders Traded Its Elections Anyway

Maryland law is not ambiguous. Election Law Section 16-902 says a person may not bet on the outcome of an election: a misdemeanor, a fine of $50 to $500, and the stake forfeited to the county. In March the State Board of Elections warned that gambling on elections is illegal in Maryland.

The markets traded anyway. As of about 9:15 AM ET on Sunday, Polymarket's 20 Maryland markets had recorded about $599,500 in volume, covering the governor's race, all eight House districts, turnout, margins and a redistricting measure. The busiest was the 1st District at about $98,800, with Rep. Andy Harris at about 86.5% against about 12% for Dan Schwartz. The governor's market carried about $30,500, with Gov. Wes Moore at about 99%.

Kalshi tells the same story in contracts: about 400,500 traded across 27 Maryland events. The governor market alone traded about 303,000 — about 199,000 on Republican nominee Dan Cox and about 104,000 on Moore, Cox last at 1 cent and Moore at 99 cents, with about 70,900 Cox contracts changing hands in the prior 24 hours. A one-cent longshot piles up contracts without piling up cash.

The state is escalating. Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis asked the state prosecutor in July to investigate whether the contracts violate the ban, and in September the board barred election officials, judges and contractors from holding them. Kalshi disputes that state law applies, saying a regulator and a Washington court have determined these markets are legal under the federal system.

Two days before the vote, Maryland is the national fight in miniature: the state is also litigating Kalshi's sports contracts, while CNN estimates 2026 election trading on Kalshi and Polymarket at more than $750 million. The ban is on the books. So are the prices.

Sources: RG, Capital Gazette, Maryland Matters

items.title: 44 Ways to Know the Answer: The Insider Problem Inside Election Markets
items.body:
44 Ways to Know the Answer: The Insider Problem Inside Election Markets

The hardest contracts in this election are not who wins. They are the ones somebody already knows. Researchers call them knowable markets: contracts on candidate withdrawals, endorsements, debate appearances and rally remarks. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective counts an average of 44 of them tied to each individual race, and they have already traded more than $20 million.

The warning case is Maine. Researchers flagged dozens of suspicious, highly correlated trades on a Kalshi contract on whether Graham Platner would drop out of the Senate race, placed just before a damaging scandal became public. The trades do not prove insider trading, but they show the shape of the risk: the narrower the question, the fewer people hold the answer.

The exchanges are answering with enforcement. Kalshi told CNN it has suspended at least six 2026 candidates for betting on their own races, and its midterm transparency recap detailed four congressional cases: Mark Moran fined $6,229.30, Matt Klein $539.85 and Ezekiel Enriquez $784.20, each with five-year bans, and Laurie Buckhout just under $2,600 with a three-year suspension.

Washington is moving too. On October 5, Representative Don Davis introduced the No Betting on Your Own Race Act, with a penalty of $10,000 or three times the net gain, whichever is larger. Polymarket says it has hired a former FBI official to lead investigations and regularly refers cases to the Justice Department.

Two days out, that is the credibility trade. A market on who wins Congress aggregates thousands of strangers. A market on what one campaign does next can be settled by a handful of insiders, and everyone pricing it knows the difference.

Sources: CNN, Bonus, The Agent Bets, Anti-Corruption Data Collective

One Market Maker, Both Exchanges: Jump Trading Took a Piece of Each

Jump Trading, one of the biggest proprietary trading firms in the world, will reportedly gain stakes in both Kalshi and Polymarket in exchange for providing liquidity on the two exchanges. The terms differ by venue: a set amount of equity in Kalshi, while the Polymarket stake can expand over time if Jump meets certain capacity-providing objectives.

Liquidity is the unglamorous problem prediction markets have to solve. Market makers keep spreads tight and keep thin, less-heralded contracts functional until other traders arrive, and bringing in third-party firms also answers the concern that an operator's own internal desk is taking the other side of retail trades. Susquehanna, a Jump rival, has been making markets for prediction firms since 2024.

The prize is pricing. Sports contracts drive the industry's volume growth, yet through the 2025 NFL season pricing on Kalshi's NFL derivatives was consistently worse than what bettors found on DraftKings and FanDuel. Deeper professional liquidity is how the exchanges close that gap.

Small stakes here are not small money. The deals come days after Kalshi closed a $1 billion Series G at a $40 billion valuation, up from $22 billion in May, with Polymarket valued at $21 billion in its last round. As the reporting notes, even an unconfirmed half-percent stake in either company would be worth tens of millions of dollars. Kalshi already counts 500 institutional entities, a quarter of its volume outside market makers.

Jump is part of a pattern: CME Group partners on the DraftKings and FanDuel event-contract platforms, NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange is Polymarket's largest investor, and Goldman Sachs calls the segment compelling. Wall Street's price-makers no longer just want to trade on these exchanges. They want to own a piece of them.

items.body:
The Downside Is the Favorite: Bitcoin's November Ladder Leans to $72,500

November opened with Bitcoin's monthly ladder leaning down, not up. Polymarket's market asking what price Bitcoin will hit in November, which closes December 1 at 12:00 AM ET, prices a fall to $72,500 at 47 percent against a rise to $85,000 at 42 percent, on $171K traded in the last 24 hours. The downside leg is the favorite in the market's biggest monthly question.

Kalshi's separate question, how high Bitcoin gets in November, tells the same story in softer form. Traders there price Bitcoin above $82,500 at 57 percent, but above $87,500 at only 26 percent, in a market closing November 30 at 11:59 PM ET. A modest new high for the month is likely, on those prices. A breakout is not.

Ethereum mirrors the lean. Its November hit market, on $61K traded in 24 hours, prices a fall to $2,100 at 57 percent against a rise to $2,500 at 48 percent. On both of the two largest coins, the first big level traders expect to be touched this month is below the current price, not above it.

The near term is less bearish. Kalshi prices Bitcoin at $78,000 or above on November 6 at 5 PM ET at 51 percent, and $78,500 or above at 45 percent, on $76K traded in 24 hours. Its end-of-2026 range market puts the likeliest band at $75,000 to $79,999.99 at 18 percent, just ahead of $80,000 to $84,999.99 at 17 percent.

That caution is trading in size. DeFi Rate counts $164M of crypto contracts traded in 24 hours, and crypto is 12 percent of all prediction-market trading. For November, that money is not chasing a rally. It is pricing a dip first.

items.title: On NFL Sunday, Football Came Fourth: Esports and the NBA Took the Board
items.body:
On NFL Sunday, Football Came Fourth: Esports and the NBA Took the Board

It is an NFL Sunday, and on Polymarket the football is not where the money is. Of the ten highest-volume markets in the last 24 hours, not one is an NFL game. The board belongs to esports and basketball: Hanwha Life Esports against Bilibili Gaming drew $7.4 million in 24 hours, on $7.8 million traded in total, ahead of every American football contract on the platform.

The chasing pack tells the same story. Karmine Corp against Movistar KOI drew $4.5 million in 24 hours, Dota 2's Team Yandex against Team Spirit drew another $4.5 million, and the NBA's Cavaliers against Bucks drew $3.1 million, on $3.9 million in total. Three different sports, none of them the one filling stadiums this afternoon.

The contrast is sharpest across venues. On the cross-venue most-traded list, the busiest NFL game market, the Jets as 54 percent favourites, drew $2.4 million in 24 hours, and the Lions at 63 percent drew $2.0 million. A single League of Legends series on Polymarket traded roughly three times the busiest NFL game market.

This is the new shape of a sports Sunday. Polymarket counted 716 active markets and $195.5 million traded in 24 hours, $4.9 billion in total, and the flow follows start times around the world, not one league's calendar. Football still owns the afternoon in America. On the exchange, it now has to queue.

Sources: PredScope, CoinStats

items.title: Five Months Old, $14.9 Billion in a Month: Polymarket US Arrived
items.body:
Five Months Old, $14.9 Billion in a Month: Polymarket US Arrived

Polymarket US launched on May 27, 2026. In October alone it traded $14.9 billion in contracts, its biggest month yet and roughly 40 percent of the $36.9 billion it has handled in its entire life. The regulated US arm is no longer a pilot. It is a market.

The last 30 days tell the story: $14.6 billion in contracts traded, $3.4 billion in dollars actually paid, across 10.9 million trades. That is up 62 percent from the 30 days before, good for a 12 percent share of all prediction-market volume, second only to Kalshi at 76 percent, while its international sibling holds 4 percent.

The peak came on October 24, a record $811 million day, inside a record $4.1 billion week from October 23 to 29. October 31 closed at $669 million, still 83 percent of that record. Open interest ended October at $77 million, up 233 percent in 30 days, and traders now work an average of 13,000 markets a day at an average trade of $315.

Sports did the heavy lifting, $14.3 billion of the 30-day total, but the fastest growth sits elsewhere: crypto volume rose 212 percent to $165 million and weather rose 154 percent to $34 million. A five-month-old exchange just posted a month most venues never reach. The question for November is no longer whether Polymarket US belongs. It is how much of Kalshi's 76 percent it takes next.

items.title: 70 Percent for a Sweep: Two Days Out, the Market Picked a Side
items.body:
70 Percent for a Sweep: Two Days Out, the Market Picked a Side

Two days before polls open on Tuesday, November 3, the balance-of-power market has stopped hedging. Kalshi put a Democratic sweep of both chambers at about 70 percent on Sunday morning, and Polymarket put it at 72 percent. A year ago that same outcome was priced at one in four, and on Kalshi it was still below 50 percent in early September.

The alternative is now the long shot. Democrats taking the House while Republicans hold the Senate stood at 27 percent on Kalshi and 23 percent on Polymarket. A Republican sweep was priced at 6.7 percent on Kalshi and 5 percent on Polymarket. Republicans control both chambers today, with a 53-47 edge in the Senate and a narrow House majority.

The chamber contracts tell the same story. Kalshi traders put Democratic control of the Senate at roughly 72 percent, up 7 points in the past week, and House control at about 94 percent for Democrats. Traders put $16 million into election markets in the past 24 hours alone, as the final weekend repriced the Senate race by race.

The scale is what makes this cycle different. The balance-of-power question alone has traded 56.2 million contracts, with 44.7 million still open, across a midterm board of 286 tradeable contracts covering all 35 Senate races and 66 competitive House districts. This is no longer a side market watching the election. It is pricing it, contract by contract, into Tuesday night.

Sources: TradingView, DeFi Rate, PredictionMarketsPicks

items.title: Sent Back to Frankfort: Kentucky Wins the First Round on Home Turf
items.body:
Sent Back to Frankfort: Kentucky Wins the First Round on Home Turf

The most consequential prediction-market ruling this month is about an address. On October 14, Magistrate Judge Edward B. Atkins signed a 14-page report recommending that Kentucky's gambling suit against Polymarket's U.S. exchange be sent back to the Franklin Circuit Court in Frankfort, where it was filed. A matching recommendation is reported in the Commonwealth's case against Kalshi. Neither is final: the parties had 14 days to object, and district judges will decide.

The stakes sit inside the complaints. Attorney General Russell Coleman filed both suits on June 17: four counts against Polymarket, and a 16-count complaint against five Kalshi entities plus Robinhood, Webull and Coinbase, seeking injunctions, civil penalties of up to $2,000 per violation and treble the value of money lost. Both sets of defendants removed the cases to federal court within two days.

They lost the forum on a ruling from September 25, when the Sixth Circuit held that Kalshi's sports contracts are not swaps, and that federal law would not preempt state gambling law even if they were. That answer binds Kentucky, Ohio, Tennessee and Michigan. Policing its own exchange, Atkins reasoned, is compliance with the law, not work as a federal officer - and preemption is a defence, which cannot support removal. Removal had already failed in Michigan, Nevada, Washington and Massachusetts.

Forum is not a technicality, because state court is where the remedies live. In Washington, after remand in May, a King County judge ordered sports markets out and Kalshi geofenced the state under threat of $120,000 a day. Kentucky's treble-damages count can reach five years of losses. One federal case remains: the CFTC's own suit against Kentucky, filed June 23 as its ninth state action - but a proposed October 9 rule writing event contracts into the swap definition does not change the statute the Sixth Circuit already read.

The industry spent 2026 arguing its contracts are federal instruments. In Kentucky, that argument now has to be made to a state judge, under state law, in the state capital.

Sources: iGaming Times, Gambling Insider, Deadspin

items.title: Six Candidates Bet on Themselves: The Knowable Market Problem
items.body:
Six Candidates Bet on Themselves: The Knowable Market Problem

The hardest trade to police in this election is the one where the trader already knows the answer. Kalshi has suspended at least six 2026 candidates this year for betting on their own races, in violation of platform rules, and says it screens every trade for suspicious timing and coordinated activity.

The clearest case is North Carolina. In August, Kalshi suspended Republican congressional candidate Laurie Buckhout for three years after she purchased less than $1,000 in contracts tied to her own race, and imposed a $2,589.96 penalty. Buckhout's own verdict was blunt: "I bet on myself. Literally." Earlier in 2026, three other congressional candidates drew five-year suspensions for the same conduct.

The risk is wider than win-or-lose contracts. An Anti-Corruption Data Collective analysis found more than $20 million traded on super-specific "knowable" midterm markets - candidate withdrawals, endorsements, debate mentions and rally locations - with an average of 44 granular markets tied to each individual race. This summer a White House teleprompter operator settled a civil probe over mention-market trades for $65,000.

Washington is now writing the rule into law. Rep. Don Davis, Buckhout's opponent, introduced the No Betting on Your Own Race Act on October 5: a $10,000 penalty or three times the gain, whichever is higher, covering candidates, spouses, dependent children and campaign committees. The House is not expected to resume regular voting until November 9, six days after Election Day, so the ban cannot arrive before this cycle ends.

Sources: CNN, Crypto News, PredictionAuthority

items.title: Traders Beat the Models 133 to 31: Weather Is a Market Now
items.body:
Traders Beat the Models 133 to 31: Weather Is a Market Now

The forecast now has a price. Kalshi runs a market on each day's high temperature in 24 US cities, and a tracker that puts every market next to 82 weather model runs and the live thermometer reading that settles it found a clear winner in the first week: the traders were better forecasters in 133 of 164 markets.

Today's sharpest fight is Oklahoma City. Traders favor a high of 71 degrees or below at 61 cents, while the models lean toward 74 to 75 degrees at 33 percent and give the traders' pick only 13 percent, a 48-point gap between money and models. Austin is nearly as split: traders price 85 to 86 degrees at 60 cents, while the models favor 81 to 82 at 30 percent.

The pattern repeats across the board. In Washington, DC, traders price 65 to 66 degrees at 74 cents against a model reading of 40 percent for the same band. In New York City, traders favor 60 to 61 degrees at 55 cents while the models put that band at 37 percent. In Atlanta, both sides agree it stays cool, but traders are firmer: 63 degrees or below at 92 cents against the models at 84 percent.

That is the point of a weather market. A forecast model gives one answer for free; a market makes thousands of people pay to be wrong. When traders beat 82 model runs in 133 of 164 markets in a single week, the thermometer stops being just a weather story and becomes a scoreboard, settled every afternoon, city by city.

Sources: Weather Markets, Kalshi

items.title: An Index for Everything: S&P Wants to Price the Future
items.body:
An Index for Everything: S&P Wants to Price the Future

The most important benchmark in finance is getting into the prediction business. On October 26, S&P Dow Jones Indices, the firm behind the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average, signed a multi-year partnership with Kalshi to build indices composed of Kalshi event contracts, and to let Kalshi list contracts on the S&P 500, the Dow and other S&P benchmarks that settle directly to official index data.

The scale of the incumbent is the point. By the end of 2024, more than $20 trillion was indexed or benchmarked to the S&P 500 alone. The Dow dates to 1896 and the S&P 500 to 1957. The new indices will bundle related event contracts, covering political power, supply chain risk, AI's impact on employment, sports outcomes and weather, into single indicators, the way a stock index bundles companies.

It is not the only door into finance opening. Rothera, the exchange owned 45 percent each by Robinhood and Susquehanna, has won CFTC approval for the first swap tied to a listed company's key performance indicator, starting with Tesla's earnings per share. The approval opens three families: financial reporting, covering earnings, sales, margins and expenses; platform usage, covering active users, customers, flights and trips; and production, covering units produced and delivered, rolling out gradually this autumn.

Kalshi is building from the other side, too: on October 6 it launched a perpetual future on 500 large U.S. companies, and last week it added sector KPI markets tracking corporate metrics across industries. Prediction markets began by pricing elections and games. Now they are pricing the earnings calendar, and Wall Street's own benchmark house is helping them do it.

items.title: Ten Platforms, Zero Compliance: Ohio Goes to Court
items.body:
Ten Platforms, Zero Compliance: Ohio Goes to Court

On October 2, the Ohio Casino Control Commission sent cease-and-desist letters to ten prediction market platforms, ordering them to halt sports event contracts for users in the state: Coinbase, Gemini Titan, MooMoo Financial, Novig, Plus500US, Polymarket, ProphetX, Robinhood Derivatives, Underdog and WeBull Financial. Each had 14 days, until October 16, to confirm compliance in writing. None did, and Governor Mike DeWine has now said the state will file suit.

Ohio is not bluffing from a weak hand. On September 25, the Sixth Circuit ruled unanimously in KalshiEx LLC v. Schuler that the Commodity Exchange Act neither applies to sports event contracts nor preempts Ohio's sports gaming law, rejecting the federal preemption argument the platforms rely on. Kalshi, fined $5 million by Ohio in April 2026 and already under a separate court order, asked the full Sixth Circuit to rehear the case on October 16. That petition is pending.

The threatened penalties are blunt: fines equal to the entire value of contracts offered to Ohioans, with unlicensed sports gaming treated as a felony that can constitute bookmaking, and officers, directors and parent companies in scope. Ohio has licensed sports betting since 2023; none of the ten holds a commission license. DeWine has called the products nothing more than gambling.

The map, though, is split. The same day Ohio sent its letters, a federal judge in Illinois ruled the opposite way, finding Kalshi's sports contracts are likely swaps under federal law. Kalshi and Polymarket have reportedly spent a combined $3 million fighting state restrictions. Ohio's suits will be the first real test of whether a state can enforce its gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges.

items.title: 87 Percent to Win, Three Spreads to Choose: Sunday's Margin Trade
items.body:
87 Percent to Win, Three Spreads to Choose: Sunday's Margin Trade

The winner is not really in dispute anywhere. For the 1 p.m. ET kickoff on Sunday, November 1, Kalshi has Cincinnati at 87%, Polymarket at 86%, DraftKings at -675 and the Dimers model at 87%, with a projected score of Bengals 30, Titans 17. A 1-6 Tennessee team visiting a 4-2 Cincinnati side chasing a third straight win is priced as close to settled.

What the markets cannot agree on is the margin. Kalshi traders have made 10.5 points the centre of the spread ladder, DraftKings sits at 12.5, and Polymarket's default line is 13.5. That is a three-point spread between the spreads, and for this game that gap is the whole trade.

Kalshi's ladder shows where the money is fighting. The 10.5-point contract has traded more than 650,000 contracts, far more than any other rung, at 55%. The ladder grades the blowout step by step: 7.5 points at 62%, 13.5 at 47%, 17.5 at 34% and 23.5 at 20%. On the 14-point win itself the rivals agree almost exactly: Polymarket prices 13.5 at 48% Yes and Kalshi at 47%. They disagree on which line to put in front of you, not on the probability.

The rest of the board fills in the shape. The total over 46.5 points sits at 50% on both Kalshi and Polymarket, Kalshi prices the Bengals over 29.5 points at 53%, and Polymarket prices the Titans over 16.5 at 52%. To score a touchdown, Chase Brown leads at 57% on Kalshi, Ja'Marr Chase follows at 52%, and Tony Pollard is the first Titan at 40%.

So Sunday offers two different trades in one game: a winner priced at 87 cents, and a margin nobody can pin to within three points. The model puts the median result right on 13.5, which is why that line is the one priced as a coin flip.

Sources: Rocky Top Insider, Dimers

items.title: Crypto Is Now Number Two: $2.7 Billion in a Single Week
items.body:
Crypto Is Now Number Two: $2.7 Billion in a Single Week

Crypto just became the second-biggest business in prediction markets. Crypto-related volume on Kalshi and Polymarket reached a record $2.7 billion in a single week in mid-October 2026, and that total makes crypto the second most traded category on both platforms, behind only sports.

Bitcoin did most of the work. Kalshi's Bitcoin contracts alone generated over $2 billion in that one week, the bulk of the combined $2.7 billion, and the standout product is its 15-minute up-or-down contract on Bitcoin. One short-duration contract family now moves more in a week than most categories move in a month.

The challenger is moving too. Polymarket's US arm reported 15-minute Bitcoin volume of about $92 million to $101 million in its first full week of operation. The crypto surge sits inside a record month at Kalshi, whose peak week of October 5 to 11 reached $19.03 billion in total contract volume across every category, with daily volume regularly between $3.9 billion and $4.4 billion.

The tell is what traders are choosing. The record arrived while spot trading volumes across crypto decline, and larger players such as Coinbase are expanding into prediction markets to find the engagement spot trading no longer delivers. A 15-minute contract rewards speed and punishes hesitation: this is exposure to volatility in tiny increments, not long-term ownership, and $2.7 billion a week says that is now the product traders want.

Sources: CryptoBriefing, TradingView

items.title: Spider-Man at 92 Percent: The Box-Office Race Ended Before the Challenger Opened
items.body:
Spider-Man at 92 Percent: The Box-Office Race Ended Before the Challenger Opened

On Halloween night, with two months of the year still to run, the market for 2026 at the movies is effectively settled. Polymarket's "Highest grossing movie in 2026?" contract, open since November 12, 2025, has traded $17.8 million across 14 possible winners, and it prices Spider-Man: Brand New Day at 92 percent.

The challenger is not close. Avengers: Doomsday sits at about 9 percent, while Wicked: For Good and Wuthering Heights are both under 1 percent. That gap holds even though Doomsday is tracking toward $100 million in presales alone, outpacing Spider-Man's presales by 67 percent in the tracking cited on the market page.

The calendar is the trade. The market resolves on Box Office Mojo's domestic calendar gross for 2026, so only money a film earns by December 31 counts. Spider-Man opened on July 29 and has had months to bank its total. Doomsday opens in December and gets roughly two weeks inside the window, no matter how large its opening weekend is.

The price tells the year's story. Spider-Man traded at just 32 percent on March 12, climbed through 83 percent in late October, and now sits at 92. A Nintendo sequel that once contended fell from 46 percent to 1 percent between March 13 and July 27. Final settlement waits for the December 31 data, due by January 7, 2027.

A movie question drawing $17.8 million is the point. Culture is no longer a side board on prediction markets; on the biggest film question of the year, the crowd has already called the winner.

Sources: Polymarket, RG, GambleRss

items.title: Half of Google's Midterm Answers Are Now a Market
items.body:
Half of Google's Midterm Answers Are Now a Market

Ask Google who will win the Senate this November, and there is an even chance a market is part of the answer. A CasinoReviews.net study of 140 Google results pages across 14 US cities found Polymarket or Kalshi on page one for half of everyday forecast searches such as "election forecast" and "midterm polls."

On 112 mobile results pages, 50% showed a betting platform on page one. The platforms appeared in all eight cities tested in states where state law bans betting on elections - Houston, Phoenix, Atlanta, Philadelphia, Detroit, Charlotte, Las Vegas and Chicago - even though 24 states ban election betting outright, while federally regulated markets still offer election contracts nationwide.

The split is sharp. Kalshi appeared on all 28 pages for "senate odds" and "midterm odds," but on only 6% of forecast pages - Kalshi owns odds searches, Polymarket owns forecasts, the study found. Searchers treat markets like polls: "Polymarket polls" and "Kalshi polls" rank among the top related searches.

Yet only about 1 in 120 midterm searches uses betting or odds language, and forecast searches without that language outnumber them nearly nine to one. Across 46 states, Google Trends interest in Polymarket and Kalshi, relative to interest in the 2026 elections, showed no consistent difference between ban states and states with no such law.

Researchers checked 10 searches in each of 14 cities on October 15 and 16, 2026, with search volumes from Ahrefs covering 10,092 US keywords containing "midterm elections." Lead researcher Nikoleta Kuncheva put it plainly: most people who search for midterm predictions are not looking to place a bet - they want to know who is going to win.

Sources: CasinoReviews.net, BusinessWire

items.title: From 27% to the Lead: Israel's $82 Million Market Flipped
items.body:
From 27% to the Lead: Israel's $82 Million Market Flipped

Before Israel voted on October 27, the market had a clear favorite. On Polymarket, Gadi Eizenkot stood at 58% to be the next prime minister and Benjamin Netanyahu at 27%. Kalshi told the same story, at 52% for Eizenkot against 28% for Netanyahu, with no other candidate close.

The votes changed the board. Netanyahu now leads the same Polymarket market at 43%, with Eizenkot at 35%, in a market that has traded $82.2 million across 19 outcomes since it opened on November 14, 2025. DeFi Rate's movers board puts Netanyahu up 15 points in seven days, from 28% to 43%.

The market is not settled, because the job goes to whoever is sworn in, and that takes 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Neither bloc had a clear path to 61 in the final polls. Official results are due November 4, and the leader chosen then gets 28 days to form a government, plus up to 14 more.

The flip also drew scrutiny. Polymarket is investigating hundreds of accounts created less than an hour before polls closed at 10 p.m. in Jerusalem, Casino.org reported on October 30. The fresh wallets jointly netted over $100,000 after exit polls favored Netanyahu, one account turned $14,000 staked 12 minutes before the close into $42,000, and analysts at Polysights put potential payouts from fresh wallets at over $700,000.

It is a clean test of what these markets price: not vote share, but coalition math after the count. The $82 million board got the favorite wrong before the vote and repriced in days. Whether it also had to police its own tape is now part of the story.

Sources: Polymarket, DeFi Rate, Casino.org, RG.org

items.title: 91 Percent at Fight Time: Canelo's Market Left the Bookies Behind
items.body:
91 Percent at Fight Time: Canelo's Market Left the Bookies Behind

On fight day in Riyadh, the prediction market stopped treating Canelo Alvarez's comeback as a contest. CoinStats' Saturday evening board read, at 7:11 PM ET, priced Canelo as the favourite at 91 percent on Kalshi, with $5.2 million traded in 24 hours on that venue and $6.6 million in total volume on the market, which resolves November 1. Hours earlier, the same contract sat at 74 percent on just $296K traded. Fight day did not nudge the price. It ran it over.

The stakes explain the rush. Canelo, 36 and 63-3-2, was fighting for the first time since losing to Terence Crawford in September 2025, and he was the challenger this time: unbeaten WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli, 29-0-1 with 24 knockouts, held the belt on the Mexico vs. The World card in Riyadh.

The striking gap was between the two kinds of market. Sportsbooks kept the upset alive all week: BetMGM had Canelo at -300, the best bookmaker price was 2/5, an implied chance of about 71 percent, and Mbilli was available at 13/5. Kalshi's traders, putting up millions on the day itself, priced the same comeback at 91 percent, near certainty.

The whole card traded, not just the main event. On Kalshi's undercard board, Jaime Munguia was -900 against Nikita Zon, a 90 percent implied chance, Rafael Espinoza was the biggest favourite on the card at -1567, and David Picasso was -355 against Carl Martin.

Boxing's biggest name now trades like a stock on fight day, and the exchange, not the bookmaker, posted the boldest number in the building.

Sources: CoinStats, Kalshi, Oddschecker, USA Today

items.title: Worth More Than the Bookies Combined
items.body:
Worth More Than the Bookies Combined

Prediction markets now have a profit story to match the volume story. In a research report released Friday, PitchBook estimates Kalshi is on course for $1.2 billion in adjusted earnings in 2026, ahead of DraftKings' guidance for the year, on $3.7 billion in gross revenue. Kalshi has already banked $2.4 billion in fee revenue before rebates this year, with records falling regularly since football season began.

The valuations are the headline. PitchBook puts Kalshi at $42.3 billion and Polymarket at $20.6 billion, a combined $62.9 billion, while Flutter and DraftKings together are worth less than $23 billion after their share prices tumbled. The estimates sit just above the roughly $40 billion and $20 billion levels the two exchanges are reportedly raising funds at, and PitchBook says the acceleration in trading volume warrants them.

The gap between the rivals is earnings, not attention. Polymarket's projected 2026 gross revenue is $842 million, with $526.9 million net and just $34.9 million in adjusted earnings, weighed down by running two exchanges, one in the U.S. and one globally. Marketing is the biggest expense at both firms, about 33 percent of Kalshi's revenue, with all of Kalshi's costs adding up to about 60 percent of revenue.

PitchBook expects the lead to widen, then narrow. By 2028 it projects Kalshi gross revenue of $8.5 billion and adjusted earnings of $3 billion, against Polymarket gross revenue of $3.2 billion and earnings of $624.3 million. Even if a court ruling cost them a quarter of U.S. sports contracts, Kalshi would still be worth $25 billion and Polymarket $14.6 billion: hurt, not ruined.

The engine underneath is volume. Kalshi set a record $5.3 billion day on a recent Saturday, a $10 billion weekend, and $25.5 billion across the seven days to October 26, taking $118.4 million in fee revenue that week. Polymarket US set its own record the same Saturday at $811.2 million. The bookies are no longer the biggest business in the room.

Sources: InGame, PitchBook

items.title: Gold Joins the 15-Minute Club: Polymarket's First Market Beyond Crypto
items.body:
Gold Joins the 15-Minute Club: Polymarket's First Market Beyond Crypto

Polymarket's fastest markets no longer stop at crypto. Its 15-minute gold and silver up-or-down markets are now live, the platform's first contracts outside crypto prices, with Chainlink as the official oracle supplying the pricing for every window.

The format is familiar, the asset is not. Traders buy shares on whether gold or silver closes a rolling 15-minute window above or below the level printed at the open. At spot near $3,980 an ounce, even a $20 move inside a window is just half a percent — a volatility contract, not a claim on the metal itself.

The scale behind the launch is the story. Chainlink and Polymarket say the partnership has already settled more than $11 billion in trading volume across Polymarket's 5- and 15-minute crypto markets. That is about 1.24 times LINK's entire market capitalization of about $8.9 billion, with LINK near $11.59 on October 31, up about 4.9 percent in 24 hours.

The crypto machine it extends is relentless: 15-minute markets settle 96 times a day, crypto accounts for $197 million traded in 24 hours on the DeFi Rate board, and Bitcoin finished up in just 49 percent of its last 1,311 Kalshi windows — 642 of them — a near coin flip where price, not direction, decides the trade.

Gold and silver are only the first step. The stated roadmap is more commodities, with equities and foreign exchange to follow, on a Polymarket US venue that operates as a CFTC-regulated designated contract market. The 15-minute club just opened its doors to traditional assets.

Sources: KuCoin, Chainlink, DeFi Rate, CoinGecko

250 Million Contracts: Three Days Out, the Election Is a Market

Three days before the Nov. 3 midterms, Kalshi's election markets have traded 250,174,205 contracts across the Senate, House and chamber-control questions, with 170,454,349 contracts still open. In the last 24 hours alone, 17,483,253 contracts changed hands across 100 live races and 310 tradeable contracts.

The balance-of-power market is the biggest single bet: 54.3 million contracts traded and 42.8 million open on the four ways Congress can split. Traders price a Democratic sweep of both chambers at 71 percent on Kalshi, and a 10,000-run simulation of today's race prices gives Democrats and independents Senate control in 71.4 percent of outcomes, with a median result of 52 to 48.

The tightest race tells the real story. In Iowa, Ashley Hinson leads at 56 cents in a market that has traded 8.0 million contracts with 4.8 million open — the highest-volume Senate race the market still cannot call. Michigan is the tipping point: call it for the Democrat and Senate control rises to 75.0 percent in the simulation; call it for the Republican and it falls to 63.4 percent.

That is what a market adds to a poll. Not a single number for Tuesday, but a live map of where control actually turns — priced, open, and still moving with three days to go.

items.title: 97 Percent to Win, 51 Percent to Cover: Notre Dame's Two Markets
items.body:
97 Percent to Win, 51 Percent to Cover: Notre Dame's Two Markets

Notre Dame against Navy is the second most traded market on the board today, with $3.3 million traded in 24 hours across two venues on DeFi Rate's top-50 list. On Kalshi alone the game has drawn about $2.9 million, and the winner is not really in doubt: Notre Dame at 97 percent, Navy at 3 percent.

Then the market splits. Notre Dame winning by more than 30.5 points sits at just 51 percent on Kalshi — a coin flip. The game total tells the same story, with over 55.5 points at 47 percent. Traders are certain who wins on this Halloween Saturday. They have almost no idea by how much, or how it looks.

It is the pattern across the whole Saturday slate. Georgia is at 80 cents against Florida at 21 cents on Kalshi, Ohio State at 69 cents against USC at 32 cents, and Texas Tech at 63 cents against Arizona at 38 cents. The favorites are clear everywhere. The margins are tight everywhere: Texas Tech by 4 or more is only 51 cents.

That split is what makes a game a market instead of a poll. A moneyline can sit at 97 percent and still leave the real trading — the spread, the total, the size of the win — wide open at fifty-fifty. On a Saturday when sports hold 34 of the top 50 markets and $29 million of $47 million in 24-hour volume, the most honest price in college football today is not 97. It is 51.

Sources: DeFi Rate, SportsBettingDime, SportsLine, Action Network

items.title: Two Exchanges, One Point Apart: The Rivals Agree
items.body:
Two Exchanges, One Point Apart: The Rivals Agree

Two rival exchanges, two different trader bases, and almost the same answer. A side-by-side comparison on October 31 matched 10 events listed on both Polymarket and Kalshi, covering 54 outcomes. Across all of them, the average gap was just 1.0 percentage point.

The biggest markets are the tightest. Democrats to win the House are at 94.5 percent on Polymarket and 93.8 percent on Kalshi, a gap of 0.7 points. Democrats to win the Senate are at 71.5 percent against 70.5 percent, a gap of 1.0. A 25-point Fed hike in December is at 70.5 percent against 69.5 percent, also 1.0.

The exceptions prove how narrow the band is. The widest gap in the whole set is Republicans to win the 2028 presidential election, at 34.5 percent on Polymarket and 40.5 percent on Kalshi, 6.0 points apart. U.S. recession by the end of 2026 is next at 6.5 percent against 2.5 percent, and even there the rules differ between the two venues.

In sports the agreement is exact in places. The Buffalo Bills are at 11.5 percent on both exchanges, the Los Angeles Rams at 6.5 percent on both, and Bayern Munich and Arsenal are level on both in the Champions League market.

That is what a maturing market looks like. Different order books, fees and access rules still leave room for a gap, and a gap is not free money. But when two rivals price 54 outcomes within a point on average, the price is no longer one exchange's opinion. It is the consensus.

Sources: PolymarketTrader, DeFi Rate

One wallet just became the midterm market. On Polymarket, a trader listed as ndb1 placed three linked positions in a single day totaling about $1.4 million, each one sized large enough to dominate its market's daily flow.

The biggest was $557,000 bought at 31 cents on which party will win the Senate in 2026, a stake equal to 19.4 percent of that market's 24-hour volume. The same wallet added a $544,000 NO position at 93 cents on which party will win the House, and a $306,000 position at 26 cents on Balance of Power for the 2026 midterms.

Those prices sit far from the consensus board. DeFi Rate's Oct. 31 average across Kalshi and Polymarket puts Democrats at about 71 percent to win the Senate and about 94 percent to win the House, which makes ndb1's 31-cent and 26-cent entries look like deep-discount bets, not follow-the-crowd trades.

ndb1 was not alone. The same whale leaderboard shows a $208,000 Cavaliers position at 44 cents and a $199,000 Team Liquid position at 80 cents that would return about $249,000 if it wins. When one wallet can be a fifth of a market's day, its price is not just a bet. It is a signal everyone else has to trade around.

items.title: Three Exchanges, Three States, One Week: The Industry Sued Back
items.body:
Three Exchanges, Three States, One Week: The Industry Sued Back

For months, the courtroom traffic ran one way: states sued prediction markets. In the last week of October, the exchanges flipped the script. Between October 26 and 27, Nadex, Kalshi and Polymarket US each walked into a different federal court and sued a state of their own.

Polymarket US moved in Louisiana. Its operator, QCX LLC, sued Attorney General Liz Murrill and the Gaming Control Board on October 27 in the Eastern District of Louisiana, case No. 2:26-cv-02482, arguing the Commodity Exchange Act preempts state enforcement and that the state's stance violates the Commerce Clause. The complaint points to a December 5, 2025 advisory calling sports event contracts illegal gambling, and notes the state's 20 sports wagering licenses go first to in-state casino and racetrack licensees.

Kalshi took Missouri the same day. KalshiEX LLC sued Attorney General Catherine Hanaway and the Gaming Commission in the Eastern District of Missouri, case No. 4:26-cv-01860, on a single claim: federal preemption under the Supremacy Clause. Missouri's September 16 cease-and-desist called Kalshi an unlicensed sports wagering platform and gave it 14 extra days to comply; Kalshi will seek a preliminary injunction, and a restraining order if the state will not stand down.

The third front is Utah, where North American Derivatives Exchange, trading as OG.com Prediction Markets, sued Attorney General Derek Brown on October 26 in the District of Utah, case No. 2:26-cv-01056, before Judge David Barlow. A CFTC-designated contract market since 2004, Nadex launched OG.com in February 2026 and raises express, field and conflict preemption. The same week, the United States and the CFTC sued Utah themselves, days after Utah sued Kalshi on October 20, and Kalshi separately sued Louisiana officials on October 23. The CFTC is now battling 10 states in court.

One federal rulebook or fifty state ones is no longer a panel argument. It is being litigated simultaneously by the regulator and by three competing exchanges that agree on almost nothing else.

Sources: RG, CoinDesk

items.title: The Model and the Market Agree to the Point
items.body:
The Model and the Market Agree to the Point

Saturday's two biggest college football games come with a rare sight: the trading market and the simulation model are pricing them almost identically. On Kalshi, Georgia is an 80-cent favorite over Florida, with Florida at 21 cents, ahead of their 3:30 p.m. ET kickoff. SportsLine's projection model, which simulates the game 10,000 times, has Georgia winning 81% of the time — one point from the market.

The primetime game is the same story. Ohio State is priced at 69 cents on Kalshi for its trip to USC, with USC at 32 cents. The same simulation model puts Ohio State's win rate at 70%. Two venues of judgment — thousands of traders putting money down, and a model running ten thousand simulated Saturdays — landed within a single point of each other, twice in one day.

Where the certainty ends is the margin. Earlier on the slate, Notre Dame was priced near 97% to beat Navy on roughly $2.9 million of volume, yet the market gave Notre Dame only a 51% chance of winning by more than 30.5 points, and just 47% for the game to clear 55.5 total points. Miami's spread against North Carolina tells the same story, with Miami to cover 14.5 priced at 49 cents — a genuine coin flip.

That split is what makes a Saturday board worth reading. The moneyline answers who wins, and on the biggest games it now matches the computers almost exactly. The spread and total markets answer how it happens, and there the market is honestly undecided — priced at 49, 51 and 47 cents, where a single drive moves the number.

Sources: SportsLine, SportsBettingDime, Action Network

Prediction markets have left the election and the stadium and entered the laboratory. Polymarket has hosted biotech contracts since May, and on July 16 Kalshi launched a suite of markets on Phase 3 trial outcomes and full FDA approvals. Volume topped $100,000 shortly after launch across about 13 markets tied to companies including Sanofi, Eli Lilly and Gilead Sciences.

The board is still live and specific. As of October 30, Kalshi offered odds on when the FDA will approve Eli Lilly's retatrutide, while Polymarket offered odds on by what date the FDA will approve Moderna's melanoma vaccine, intismeran autogene. Pharmaceutical Technology reports users may place hundreds of thousands of dollars on outcomes like these.

The stakes explain the interest. Bringing a single drug to market costs an estimated $2.3 billion, and as of the FDA's April 2026 figures, roughly 30 percent of trials required to report results had posted none. Kalshi, working with AppliedXL, says a public contract can produce a continuously updated public probability, and it framed the markets in May as a way to help solve drug development's information silo problem.

The guardrails are part of the story. Kalshi's pilot covers only late-stage trials, lists a contract only after a trial finishes enrolling, and requires employment verification for traders in these markets. Fenwick partners Chelsea Anderson and Noah Solowiejczyk told Pharmaceutical Technology the markets are here to stay, but that private biotechs, once shielded from this exposure, now face a new insider-trading risk and likely more regulation.

items.title: Prices Get Smarter as Deadlines Get Closer
items.body:
Prices Get Smarter as Deadlines Get Closer

Prediction markets are often judged on their worst screenshot: a stale price from a thin market, quoted months early. Kalshi's August 2026 accuracy study measured the whole curve instead, and found its predictions generally became more accurate as events approached, especially in markets with more traders and more trading activity.

An independent check across nine resolved markets in politics, sports and pop culture found the same shape. An 80-cent contract that loses is not automatically a bad forecast; the other outcome carried a real 20% chance, and across many similar markets those chances are the product being sold.

The two levers in the study are the ones traders can actually see before they buy: time to resolution and crowd size. A liquid market near its deadline is a measurement. A thin market far from one is a rumor with a price tag.

Read that way, the industry's growth is itself an accuracy story. Record crowds and record volume do not just make exchanges richer. They make every number on the board harder to fool.

A 24-point gap on the cycle's biggest question is not a rounding error. The venues run different books with different crowds: Kalshi's midterm complex counts 311 tradeable contracts and tens of millions in open interest, while the Polymarket US Senate market traded just $77K in the last 24 hours.

Thin books price noisily. A $77K day can be moved by a handful of orders, while Kalshi's price is set by a crowd that has been building positions for months. When two prices disagree this much, the deeper market is usually the one quoting information; the thinner one is quoting whoever showed up today.

Election night will grade both. Until then, the gap itself is the data point: it measures how much of the prediction-market map is deep water and how much is still a puddle.

Michigan's move lands while the federal fight escalates elsewhere. The CFTC has now sued ten states over enforcement against federally regulated exchanges, arguing event contracts are swaps under federal law. States answer that sports contracts are gambling under theirs.

Until an appellate court settles it, traders should expect more lines like Michigan's: drawn quietly, enforced immediately, and different on the other side of the state line.

Ninety-Six Settlements a Day: The 15-Minute Crypto Machine

Crypto is 21% of all prediction-market trading, and most of it is not price targets or year-end ladders. It is 15-minute up-or-down markets, settling 96 times a day, recycling the same money around the clock. About $213 million traded in these windows in the 24 hours to this morning.

The mechanics are simple. Kalshi sets a target price for Bitcoin at the start of each window; finish at or above it and Up wins. This morning's 8:00 AM window used a $77,488.22 target, and the market leaned 85% Down on Kalshi while Polymarket US sat at 58% Down for the same quarter hour.

Coinbase has listed Kalshi's 15-minute and hourly crypto markets since October 6 in every state except Nevada, so a Coinbase trade and a Kalshi trade are now the same contract settling the same way, on the CF Benchmarks index.

Ninety-six settlements a day means no position is ever far from an answer. That speed is why this corner of the market now out-trades entire categories that used to define the industry.

items.title: The Weekend Clock: What to Watch After the Binance Hack
items.body:
The Weekend Clock: What to Watch After the Binance Hack

The Binance story now runs on three clocks, and all of them strike within days. First: withdrawals. In their October 30 letter, co-CEOs Yi He and Richard Teng targeted a phased resumption of withdrawals within about 34 hours, once security checks are complete — a window that points at Sunday, November 1. Binance stresses the restart will be phased, not simultaneous for every asset or account, and the exchange has not yet confirmed that withdrawals have resumed.

Second: proof of reserves. Binance planned an initial reserves snapshot within 12 hours of its update, with results due Monday, November 2. Those results have not been published yet. When they land, they are the first hard check on Binance's pledge that its $6.34 billion set-aside fully covers the theft.

Third: the coins that cannot be frozen. About $3.3 billion of the stolen assets sit outside issuer control, including 18,270 BTC split across 19 wallets, per Elliptic figures reported by Cointribune. Any move from those wallets toward an exchange is the market's clearest sell-pressure signal; Compass Point analysts are watching bitcoin's $75,000 to $77,000 range in the meantime.

Also due: Binance's fuller technical findings, expected within about 48 hours of its update, and a promised post-mortem. Until those land, the hack's final shape — how the attackers got in, and what changes because of it — is still being written.

Sources: Binance update via Forbes, CryptoBriefing, CoinDesk, Cointribune

items.title: Bitcoin Fell 4 Percent on the Biggest Hack in History
items.body:
Bitcoin Fell 4 Percent on the Biggest Hack in History

A $6.3 billion theft at the world's largest exchange knocked bitcoin down about 4 percent. In 2018, a failed attack on the same exchange — one that stole nothing — knocked it down roughly 11 percent. The difference between those two numbers is the story of how this market has changed.

Bitcoin tumbled to a six-week low of $76,368 as the news broke, then pared losses to trade near $77,300 on Friday and about $77,509 on Saturday morning, per Finnhub. Ether fell to $2,178, a two-month low, before recovering toward $2,246. Leveraged traders took the sharpest hit: about $1.5 billion in liquidations, $468 million of it in bitcoin and $358 million in ether, according to Cryptowisser.

Crypto stocks fell harder than crypto. Coinbase closed down 10.6% on October 30, Strategy fell 7.8% and Robinhood 7.2%, per DefiLlama equity data cited by Coinjuice — a reminder that the equity wrappers carry exchange risk even when the networks themselves were never breached.

Analysts split on what comes next. Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan expects bitcoin's price to recover within a week, and TD Cowen, Cantor Fitzgerald and Compass Point all called the selloff a buying opportunity. Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick is the caution, expecting pressure until the frozen assets' status clears. With a crypto market worth about $2.6 trillion and U.S. spot ETFs holding roughly 1.3 million BTC, the shock absorbers are simply bigger than in 2018.

Sources: WSJ, Cointribune, Cryptowisser, Finnhub

items.title: Half the Loot Is Frozen. The Other Half Cannot Be.
items.body:
Half the Loot Is Frozen. The Other Half Cannot Be.

The fastest number in the Binance story is not the $6.3 billion stolen. It is the roughly $3 billion frozen within hours, as the industry's biggest issuers moved in coordination: Tether froze more than $1.567 billion in USDT, Circle froze more than $800 million in USDC, and Ripple and World Liberty Financial blocked additional tokens, according to CoinDesk.

The catch is structural. Stablecoins can be frozen because an issuer controls them. Bitcoin cannot — there is no issuer to call. Arkham data cited by CoinDesk shows the attacker has already split about $1.4 billion in stolen bitcoin — 18,270 BTC — across 19 wallets, and has borrowed 20,000 wrapped ether, roughly $44 million, through Aave using stolen USDT as collateral.

Freezing is also not the same as recovery. Legal experts told CoinDesk that blocked tokens are stopped, not returned; getting them back to Binance is a separate legal process. The speed of this freeze has raised an uncomfortable question inside the industry: smaller hack victims usually wait on court orders, while the largest exchange in the world got a $3 billion freeze in hours.

That asymmetry is now part of the security debate. The breach entered through a laptop and internal systems, not stolen keys — which means the next round of exchange safeguards will be about endpoints, approvals and withdrawal controls, not just wallet architecture.

Sources: CoinDesk, Arkham

items.title: The Odds Board Priced the Hack in Hours
items.body:
The Odds Board Priced the Hack in Hours

Prediction markets did not wait for the post-mortem. Within hours of the Binance breach becoming public, Polymarket's weekly bitcoin line (October 26 to November 1) put a 46% chance on bitcoin trading at or below $76,000 before the week closes on Sunday, according to RG.org's market wrap. Bitcoin's overnight low near $76,400 came within about half a percent of that line without touching it.

The repricing was sharpest in the October contracts. Polymarket's "Bitcoin dips to $75,000 in October" market jumped from 5% to 20% as the hack landed, one of the biggest 24-hour movers on the board. Traders were pricing a second leg down, not a collapse: the recovery strikes stayed alive on the same board, and bitcoin steadied near $77,300 by Friday morning.

Kalshi's daily ladder told the same story in smaller increments. Its "What price will Bitcoin hit on October 31?" market, with $173K traded in 24 hours as observed on the morning of October 31, priced the $78,000 strike at 56%, per DeFi Rate's market data. The 15-minute up-or-down markets on both venues kept cycling through the volatility — 96 settlements a day — with Down favored in the early Saturday windows.

The board's verdict, for now: a real shock, a priced-in tail risk, and no panic premium for disaster. That changes only if the stolen coins start moving — or if withdrawals stay closed longer than promised.

Sources: RG.org, DeFi Rate, CoinDesk

items.title: Twenty Minutes, $6.3 Billion: The State of the Binance Hack
items.body:
Twenty Minutes, $6.3 Billion: The State of the Binance Hack

At about 20:05 UTC on Thursday, October 29, attackers drained an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance's hot wallets across several blockchains. Most of the coins — bitcoin, ether and stablecoins among them — left in a burst that lasted roughly 20 minutes, according to CoinDesk. It is the largest theft in crypto history, more than four times the $1.46 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025.

Binance says the entry point was a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which let the attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal requests through internal systems. The exchange says it later found additional exploit points, but has seen no evidence that any wallet private keys were stolen.

Blockchain analysts moved fast on attribution. TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group with high confidence, citing the speed and sophistication of the operation. The FBI says it is engaged with public and private partners, and the U.S. Secret Service says its investigators are working with Circle and others to trace and freeze the funds.

Two numbers now define the story. Binance has set aside more than $6.34 billion of its own resources to restore customer balances, and industry partners have frozen about $3 billion of the stolen assets. Withdrawals remain paused pending security checks; deposits remain open.

Sources: CoinDesk, CNN, TRM Labs

Two years ago Polymarket was the prediction market. It held about 95 percent of the market in September 2024 and 96 percent at its peak. That era is over. Its share has fallen to 27 percent, and Kalshi now trades nearly three times its volume.

Among U.S.-regulated platforms Kalshi held around 83 percent, Polymarket US sat at 12 to 15 percent, and Polymarket Global fell to single digits.

The money still on the table tells the same story. Kalshi carried about $2.05 billion in open interest in October, against $384 million at Polymarket US. Across all venues DeFi Rate counted $123.4 billion traded in 30 days, with Kalshi handling 76 percent of it and $4.5 billion changing hands in the last 24 hours alone.

The drivers were not luck. Kalshi chose CFTC regulation, distribution through Robinhood and Coinbase, and breadth into sports and parlay-style contracts. Polymarket US is growing faster in percentage terms, but on a $10 billion base against $65 billion, the absolute gap is still widening heading into the midterms.

items.title: Gold's Ceiling Caved In: $4,400 Went From 27% to 16%
items.body:
Gold's Ceiling Caved In: $4,400 Went From 27% to 16%

Gold was supposed to keep climbing. Prediction markets just cut the ceiling. PAX Gold trades at $3,893, down 2.24% on the day, and traders on Kalshi have slashed the odds of gold closing 2026 above $4,300 from 34% to 22%.

The higher rungs fell harder. The chance of a close above $4,400 was trimmed from 27% to 16%, and the full Kalshi ladder now puts $4,500 or above at just 14% and $5,000 or above at 10%. A market that once priced a runaway year-end is now pricing a ceiling.

The downside trade moved the other way. On Polymarket, the odds of gold falling below $3,500 doubled from 10% to 20%. That is not a crash call — it is a repricing: the tail traders ignored a week ago now carries one chance in five.

The money behind the move is real, if concentrated. The six gold markets tracked across Kalshi and Polymarket, including the flagship What will Gold hit by end of December contract, have traded over $4.56 million to date. In that flagship, hitting $4,500 at any point still sits at 49.5% — far above the 14% for closing there.

That gap is the story. Traders still think gold can spike to $4,500. They no longer think it can stay there.

items.title: Two Percent to Thirty: The Golf Longshot Who Ate the Board
items.body:
Two Percent to Thirty: The Golf Longshot Who Ate the Board

A week ago, Andrew Novak was a 2 percent afterthought in the VidantaWorld Mexico Open winner market on Kalshi. Today he leads a 123-outcome board at 30 percent, a 27-point climb that is the biggest seven-day move on DeFi Rate's prediction-market board.

The money followed the move. The market traded $800K in the last 24 hours, running at 2.2 times its daily average, and a $100 position on Novak at the ask now pays $333 if he wins. In a field this wide, one name taking nearly a third of the probability is a statement, not a drift.

The rest of the board shows how open it still is. Ben Griffin sits second at 12 percent and Marco Penge third at 5.3 percent, leaving more than half the probability spread across the other 120 golfers. Novak is the favorite now, but the market is still pricing a race, not a coronation.

Golf outrights are a hard test for any exchange. Unlike a two-team game, a 123-outcome board has to price contenders, longshots and the field at once, and keep all of those prices honest as the tournament moves. A 27-point repricing in a single week is exactly the kind of move that test is built to catch.

That is the new shape of golf on prediction markets: a 123-name outright board repricing in real time, where a longshot can gain 27 points in a week and pull $800K of fresh trading behind him.

items.title: Twelve Trades for $114.87: Utah Put Kalshi's Founders on the Charge Sheet
items.body:
Twelve Trades for $114.87: Utah Put Kalshi's Founders on the Charge Sheet

The evidence is small. The charges are not. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed a criminal complaint on October 29 naming Kalshi chief executive Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara as defendants, after an undercover agent placed 12 sports trades on the platform for a total of $114.87.

The complaint carries 12 counts of online gaming promotion plus a single count of pattern of unlawful activity. It landed less than two weeks after Utah sued Kalshi in civil court, calling gambling a public nuisance that inflicts substantial harm on state residents. Utah bans gambling outright, and Brown's position is blunt: calling a bet a prediction market, and holding a federal registration, does not put a company above state law.

Kalshi called the filing a crazy overreach and said Utah is clearly playing politics, vowing to stop it in court as it did in Arizona. Arizona was the first state to bring criminal charges against Kalshi earlier this year, and a judge later put that case on hold. The legal map is now fragmented across roughly 20 states, with federal circuit courts split on whether sports event contracts are swaps, while the CFTC has sued at least 10 states to stop them regulating the platforms.

That is what makes Utah different. Civil suits argue about jurisdiction. A felony complaint names people. The timing sharpens the contrast: the charges arrived in the same week Kalshi completed a $1 billion raise at a $40 billion valuation. A market big enough to be worth $40 billion is now big enough for prosecutors to test personally, and legal analyst Daniel Wallach calls Utah a bellwether for how other states approach Kalshi and Polymarket.

items.title: The One-Cent Shelf: $419 Million Traded on Almost Nothing
items.body:
The One-Cent Shelf: $419 Million Traded on Almost Nothing

Look at the top of the prediction-market volume board and the biggest numbers carry the smallest prices. Eight markets priced at exactly 1 cent, the floor, have traded $418,727,767 between them, according to PicksByOdds' live board on October 31. Volume, it turns out, does not require belief.

The leader is "Will Jesus Christ return before 2027?" at 1 cent on $66,761,416 traded. Next is LeBron James winning the 2028 presidential election, also 1 cent, on $54,895,306. Oprah Winfrey winning the 2028 Democratic nomination follows at 1 cent on $54,448,323, and Bernie Sanders winning the same nomination at 1 cent on $52,923,492. Those four alone account for more than $228 million.

The shelf runs deeper. Chelsea Clinton at $51,070,529, Andrew Yang at $48,953,782, Tim Walz at $44,877,007 and Hunter Biden at $44,797,912, each priced at 1 cent for the 2028 Democratic nomination or the presidency, bring the eight-market total past $418 million, none of them moving off the floor.

PicksByOdds notes much of that activity likely reflects traders selling cheap Yes shares to collect small, slow returns, not anyone expecting the outcome. A 1-cent Yes pays a dollar if it happens; the other side collects the near-certain cent, repeated at enormous scale. High volume on a longshot is still a longshot.

That is a tell about this market's maturity. The board's heaviest traffic is not always a forecast. Sometimes it is a yield trade wearing a headline, and the one-cent shelf is where prediction markets quietly became a place to park conviction that nothing will happen.

items.title: Kansas Flipped: Three Days Out, the Senate Map Moved
items.body:
Kansas Flipped: Three Days Out, the Senate Map Moved

Three days before Election Day on November 3, the biggest move on the midterm board is not in a marquee state. In Kansas, the Democrat in the Senate race climbed from 40% to 51% in seven days on Kalshi, an 11-point jump that DeFi Rate ranks as the largest Senate move of the week. At 51 cents to 50 cents, a race traders had priced as Republican is now a coin flip that broke the other way.

That one flip is why the chamber numbers keep rising. Averaging Kalshi and Polymarket, DeFi Rate puts Democrats at 70% to take the Senate and 94% to win the House, with traders putting $24 million into election markets in the past 24 hours. Kalshi alone prices Senate control at 68% and House control at 93%, across 311 tradeable midterm contracts covering 35 Senate races and 66 competitive House districts.

The path still runs through the same states. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats, and DeFi Rate notes the 51st seat runs through Maine, where Troy Jackson is at 69%. Texas has moved with Kansas: James Talarico is at 71%, up 6 points in a week. Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed is at 75%, also up 6, and Minnesota's Democrat rose from 84% to 90%.

The tightest board is Iowa, where Ashley Hinson leads Josh Turek 56 cents to 45, on 7.9 million contracts traded. And the balance-of-power combo, the single bet on who controls both chambers, has traded 77.8 million contracts with 60.9 million still open. Three days out, the House looks priced in. Kansas is the reminder that the Senate is not.
